people.summary: President of Nigeria. He removed the fuel subsidy on 1 January 2012 and defended it, calling the subsidies 'economically unsustainable' (RNZ). Petrol prices more than doubled. Announced on 16 January that his government would reduce gasoline prices. Soldiers barricaded key roads in Nigeria's two biggest cities that day; three people were killed in protests near central Lagos.

people.name: Daniel Noboa
people.summary: President of Ecuador. His Decree 126 of 12 September 2025 ended the diesel subsidy and raised prices by over 50%, per Human Rights Watch. His decree of 16 September declared a state of emergency in 7 provinces and led to the armed forces being deployed. The Alliance for Human Rights in Ecuador reported two deaths and at least 296 injured as of 18 October.

records.what: Issued Decree 126 ending the diesel subsidy; he said it cost nearly US$1.1 billion a year (HRW, 21 October 2025).

His 16 September decree suspended freedom of assembly in 7 provinces and triggered deployment of the armed forces; the Constitutional Court limited it to two provinces. A decree of 4 October covered 10 more. HRW cites three videos of people in military uniform beating Efraín Fueres, who died on 28 September; INREDH reported a gunshot wound to the back, and prosecutors opened an inquiry.

people.name: Guillermo Lasso
people.summary: President of Ecuador during the June 2022 national strike. He issued a state of emergency decree on 17 June (No. 455) and replaced it on 20 June with one covering six provinces and banning assembly in public spaces, per El Comercio. He then announced a 10-cent-a-gallon cut in petrol, reported on 27 June. Al Jazeera reported at least six killed in clashes with security forces.

records.what: Repealed Decree 455 of 17 June and issued a new decree on 20 June for Pichincha, Imbabura, Cotopaxi, Chimborazo, Tungurahua and Pastaza, restricting assembly in public spaces while allowing peaceful demonstrations; the Quito curfew stayed.
Announced the petrol cut a day after lifting the state of emergency. At least six people were reported killed in clashes with security forces.

people.name: María Paula Romo
people.summary: Ecuador's Minister of Government during the October 2019 strike. On 25 November 2020 the National Assembly censured and removed her, 104 of 134 present voting yes. people.name: Rafael Correa
people.summary: President of Ecuador. By executive decree he extended the state of exception in Morona Santiago on 12 January 2017, suspending rights including assembly and free movement (Vistazo). He said it was 'a lie' that the Nankints area was ancestral land. Police had evicted the 32 people of Nankints on 11 August 2016; no page says who ordered that.

people.name: Javier Milei
people.summary: President of Argentina. He vetoed an 8.1% pension rise in September 2024 and, in August 2025, a 7.2% pension rise and related pension and disability bills. Police used pepper spray and rubber bullets outside Congress on 11 September 2024 after the lower house failed to override the first veto. Congress overrode the disability veto in 2025.

records.what: Vetoed the 8.1% rise. On 11 September 153 deputies voted against the veto and 87 for it, with 8 abstaining; that fell short of the two-thirds needed to override. Police fired pepper spray and rubber bullets at a group after the vote; TN reported at least 12 injured.
Signed three vetoes, reported on 2 August for gazette publication on 4 August: a 7.2% pension rise with a bonus of AR$110,000, a pension moratorium, and a disability emergency law.
Congress overrode the disability veto: 172 to 73 in the lower house on 20 August, 63 to 7 in the Senate on 4 September.

people.name: Patricia Bullrich
people.summary: Argentina's Security Minister at the 12 March 2025 pensioners' protest. MercoPress reports she enforced an anti-picketing protocol; 124 people were arrested. A tear gas canister fired by a gendarme struck photographer Pablo Grillo in the head. On 17 March she took responsibility for the police response. A judge ordered the gendarme prosecuted in October 2025; Bullrich is not reported as charged.

records.what: Enforced the anti-picketing protocol at the protest and barred those charged over it from football stadiums. MercoPress: at least 20 hurt, including 10 police; 124 arrested.
On 17 March took responsibility for the police response and said the officer who fired the canister followed protocol; Grillo needed two brain surgeries (CPJ).

Judge María Servini on 7 October 2025 ordered gendarme Héctor Guerrero prosecuted for very serious injuries and abuse of weapons, finding he fired horizontally and against regulations. He says he is innocent. El Cronista does not report Bullrich as charged.
A federal appeals chamber confirmed the prosecution; published 26 December 2025. La Izquierda Diario says the former minister 'ni siquiera fue citada a declarar'.
Grillo, as a private accuser, asked the court to widen the case to the chain of command and named Bullrich. Reported 10 February 2026; no ruling on it or formal charge against her is reported.
